report:
### Conclusion
The health claim is **supported by scientific evidence**. Higher consumption of olive oil—particularly extra-virgin olive oil—is consistently associated with a reduced risk of stroke in both observational studies and randomized controlled clinical trials.

### Key Evidence
1. **Randomized Clinical Trials:** The landmark PREDIMED trial evaluated individuals at high cardiovascular risk and demonstrated that adhering to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil significantly reduced primary major cardiovascular events, including stroke (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29897866/).
2. **Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses:**
   * A systematic review on dietary primary prevention of stroke showed that higher olive oil intake was associated with a significant reduction in stroke risk (RR: 0.60, 95% CI: 0.47–0.77) (https://www.academia.edu/109593807/Diet_and_primary_prevention_of_stroke_Systematic_review_and_dietary_recommendations_by_the_ad_hoc_Working_Group_of_the_Italian_Society_of_Human_Nutrition).
   * Meta-analyses synthesizing observational studies indicate that increased daily consumption of olive oil (such as 25 g/day or ~2 tablespoons) is associated with up to a 26% lower risk of stroke (https://www.myolivea.com/blogs/research/olive-oil-stroke-cardiovascular-meta-analysis-2014).
   * Broader epidemiological meta-analyses further confirm that olive oil consumption reduces overall cardiovascular disease endpoints and mortality (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2022.1041203/full).

### Underlying Mechanisms
Researchers attribute these protective effects to olive oil’s high content of monounsaturated fatty acids (principally oleic acid) and antioxidant polyphenols, which promote vascular function, reduce inflammation, and improve lipid profiles.
